items.title: 3.3.3 Applications of the VSEPR model in drug designing

source_refs.note: Topic 3.3.3, printed pages 58-59. Figure 3.21 (aspirin bound to COX, a published image) is not reproduced; the text carries the example.

blocks.text: Drugs are chemical substances that prevent, diagnose, or treat a disease. Drugs interact with human body at specific points, or with specific processes called targets or substrates, through their bioactive molecules called ligands. A receptor is mostly a protein that receives and responds to a ligand through binding. The examples of targets in the body are receptors, such as enzymes, proteins, nucleic acids, and cellular pathways. Each drug interacts with a specific target in the body to a different degree, this feature is called specificity of a drug or a ligand.

blocks.alt: Lock-and-key scheme. Two keys, A and B, above a block labelled Receptor whose notch matches key A. Equilibrium arrows lead to the receptor with key A fitted into the notch, while key B stays outside, and an arrow from the receptor points to 'Action'. Below: 'Drug A binds to receptor' and 'Drug B cannot bind to receptor'.
blocks.caption: Drug A binds to the receptor; drug B cannot bind to the receptor (original drawing after the lock-and-key scheme printed in the textbook).

blocks.text: Molecular shape is an important feature that determines how a drug interacts with a biological target. Only the ligands with suitable shape can fit in the active sites of a biological target as a specific key fits in a specific lock. VSEPR model is successfully applied in determining the shapes of various biological systems, such as substrate recognition, ligand specificity or selectivity, and antibody recognition. For example, Aspirin is an analgesic drug (painkiller) used for relief from pain as a primary medicine. It interacts with an enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase) by binding to its active site through the acetyl group (-OCCH₃).

The shape of COX active site and that of acetyl group on Aspirin are compatible with each other as in fig. 3.21. Therefore, the binding is successful to block COX, which is a cause of the pain in the body.

blocks.alt: Two green enzyme units side by side in a lipid membrane, labelled 'Platelet COX-1 dimer'. In the left unit a red dot marked 'Ser' carries a red acetyl group (O=C-CH3), with the label 'irreversible acetylation' over a red bracket. A solid arrow runs from aspirin (a benzene ring with COOH and a red O-CO-CH3 group) up into the channel, and a dashed arrow runs out to salicylic acid (a benzene ring with COOH and OH).
